flashcards.q: Quorum size formula and fault tolerance for N=3, 5, 7 in Raft.
flashcards.a: Quorum = floor(N/2)+1. N=3 -> quorum 2, tolerates 1 failure. N=5 -> quorum 3, tolerates 2 failures. N=7 -> quorum 4, tolerates 3 failures. 4 nodes tolerates only 1 failure, same as 3, which is why production clusters use odd N.

flashcards.q: Raft election timeout and heartbeat interval, from the original paper.
flashcards.a: Election timeout: randomized 150-300ms. Heartbeat interval: ~50ms (roughly 10x margin below the timeout). Production rule: election timeout should be >= 10x the measured inter-node RTT.

flashcards.q: Why is election timeout randomized rather than fixed?
flashcards.a: A fixed timeout means every follower times out simultaneously, causing repeated split votes. Randomizing (e.g. 150-300ms) means one node almost always fires first and wins the election before others become candidates.

flashcards.q: What is a Raft "term" and what role does it play?
flashcards.a: A monotonically increasing integer acting as a logical clock over leadership epochs. Every election bumps it. Any message carrying a lower term is rejected immediately, which is what makes it safe for a stale, isolated leader's heartbeats to be ignored once everyone else has moved to a higher term.

flashcards.q: Difference between "replicated" and "committed" in Raft's log.
flashcards.a: Replicated = appended to a follower's log (can be a minority). Committed = replicated to a MAJORITY, at which point it's safe to apply to the state machine and ack the client, because majority-replication guarantees survival across future leader elections.

flashcards.q: What is the Raft "election restriction" and why does it matter for safety?
flashcards.a: A candidate can only win a vote if its log is at least as up-to-date (by last-entry term, then index) as the voter's. This guarantees any future leader's log is a superset of all previously committed entries, preventing committed data loss across leader changes.

flashcards.q: Did Raft beat Paxos on power or on comprehensibility? What's the evidence?
flashcards.a: Comprehensibility, not power -- they are proven equivalent in the failure conditions under which they can make progress. Evidence: the 2014 user study of 43 students found most scored better on Raft comprehension questions than Paxos questions after learning both.

flashcards.q: What is a fencing token and where must it be enforced?
flashcards.a: A monotonically increasing number issued on every lease/leadership acquisition. Must be enforced at the STORAGE/WRITE layer (reject any write with a token lower than the last seen), not just at the lock service, or a stale paused holder can still corrupt state after waking up.

flashcards.q: What did Kleppmann's 2016 Redlock critique actually identify as missing?
flashcards.a: Redlock provides mutual exclusion under a timing assumption but produces no fencing token -- no monotonically increasing number guaranteed on each acquisition -- so nothing stops a stale, paused holder's write from landing at the storage layer even if the locking algorithm itself is otherwise sound.

flashcards.q: Lamport clock: what does C(a) < C(b) actually prove?
flashcards.a: Almost nothing on its own. If a causally precedes b, C(a) < C(b) is guaranteed, but the converse is false -- two unrelated concurrent events can get any relative counter values via arbitrary tie-breaking. Lamport gives total order, not causality detection.

flashcards.q: Why do vector clocks not scale, concretely?
flashcards.a: A vector clock carries one counter per participating node (O(n) space per event/version), and n grows with every node/client that has ever contributed and doesn't shrink without active pruning -- in high-churn systems this becomes real bandwidth/storage overhead (Dynamo's sibling version-vector bloat).

flashcards.q: How does a Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) compute its next value?
flashcards.a: Keeps a pair (physical_time, logical_counter). If wall-clock time exceeds the max of last-seen HLC values, adopt it and reset the counter to 0; otherwise keep the higher physical component and increment the counter to break ties. Gives causal ordering plus a value that stays close to real wall-clock time, at O(1) space.

flashcards.q: Which production systems use HLC and for what?
flashcards.a: CockroachDB uses HLC for transaction timestamp ordering, with an uncertainty interval equal to the configured max clock offset (default 500ms) to resolve ambiguous reads. MongoDB exposes it as ClusterTime/operationTime for causal consistency across replica sets.

flashcards.q: Why must lease/timeout code use a monotonic clock rather than wall-clock time?
flashcards.a: NTP step corrections can jump wall-clock time backward or forward discontinuously, breaking any elapsed-time calculation. A monotonic clock (e.g. CLOCK_MONOTONIC) only ever moves forward at a steady rate, which is what elapsed-duration checks (like lease expiry) actually need.

flashcards.q: Does "we use Raft" mean a system is fully split-brain proof? Why or why not?
flashcards.a: No. Raft prevents split-brain within the consensus log itself (two leaders both getting entries committed in one term). It says nothing about a stale leader's side effects issued OUTSIDE the log (e.g. calling an external API before it has stepped down), which aren't protected by term/quorum checks at all.
